newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bumper harvests weigh on EU grain prices.
newsitem.headline: Bumper harvests weigh on EU grain prices.

text.p: European Union grain prices slipped further in France and in Britain this week on pressure from bumper crops.
But German bread wheat bucked the trend, underpinned by export demand and a scarcity of top quality wheat.
In France wheat prices were unmoved after the European Commission signalled sales of subsidised EU wheat may soon resume after being suspended since last year when prices were at an all-time high.
September Rouen wheat was quoted at 875 francs per tonne, excluding carry, down from 890-895 last week but unchanged from the previous day.
On Thursday the EU scrapped a 10 Ecus tax applying since mid-July to soft and durum wheat exports, replacing it with a non-prefixable nil value refund.
It also passed a regulation preventing traders from offering to pay a tax to export wheat through the weekly tender channel.
"The Commission has given the signal tax days are over," one trader said.
But dealers cautioned this did not mean the Commission was ready to part with large tonnages of wheat nor grant substantial export refunds.
"This does not mean Brussels will give a 10 Ecu refund right away, it is just unblocking the tender system," one trader said.
Barley prices in France and Germany rose on Friday on news the Commission sold large tonnages of intervention and free-market barley at its weekly tender.

But one dealer said it was unclear at this stage if free-market barley would be used to increase the share of the EU in a large barley sale to Saudi Arabia or reduce the quota of German intervention barley earmarked for the Saudis.

Last Wednesday Alain Moulinier, director general of France's grain office ONIC, said that faced with a bumper crop the EU must boost exports of free-market barley to avoid large sales to intervention stores.
French maize was easier, undermined by competition from Spanish crops.
In Germany, Polish demand underpinned wheat export prices although no trades had been confirmed, dealers said.
Fob Baltic sellers price of German wheat was kept steady from earlier this week in a 290-320 marks/tonne range.
German millers were seen ready to accept firm domestic prices because of wheat export demand and a scarcity of top baking qualities in the weather-damaged crop.
Millers were paying 272.50-287.50 marks/tonne free mill for new crop standard bread wheat of 12.5-13 percent protein and 220-250 hagberg, 20-30 marks above prices last year.
Some 95 percent of the wheat crop in northern Germany has now been harvested. Traders said farmers were prepared to retain top qualities in the hope of firmer prices later on.
German feed wheat prices were undermined by competitive British offers but benefited from higher soymeal prices, which encouraged feed grain use.
Spot export barley prices were raised 2.00-5.00 marks to 252-265 marks Fob. Bread rye remained at just under 260 marks fob and feed rye at 245 marks fob.
Wheat prices in the UK have been easing during most of the week on pressure from bumper harvests in the UK and France.
"No one wanted to be the first to sell the market down but people now realise our prices were too high, partially in relation to the French market, and that started the slide," one trader said.

In Spain barley and maize prices held steady with a slightly higher presence of Spanish barley as farmers loosened their hold on supplies. Freak rainstorms in the southeast damaged rice crops but did not immediately affect grain prices.
